function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

Translation & Patient Coordination Services

93|

Language support, medical interpretation, and professional coordinators — and why they matter for your outcome

94|
95| ⏱️ 10 min read 96| 🛠️ Practical Level 97|
98|
99|
100| 101|
102|
103|
104|

1. Why Language Is a Medical Safety Issue

105|

Medical communication is not casual conversation. A misunderstood dosage instruction, a misread consent form, or an unclear post-operative warning — these are not inconveniences. They are patient safety risks.

106|

In China, where the healthcare system operates primarily in Mandarin, international patients face a real language gap. This gap must be professionally bridged — not left to Google Translate or hand gestures.

107|
108| 109|
110|

2. Types of Language Support Available

111| 112|

Hospital International Departments

113|

Most Tier 3 hospitals with international patient programs have English-speaking coordinators. These coordinators are not medical interpreters — they help with administrative tasks: scheduling, billing, communicating non-clinical information.

114| 115|

Medical Interpreters

116|

For actual medical consultations — understanding your diagnosis, explaining surgical risks, post-operative care instructions — you need a certified medical interpreter, not a general language translator. Key points:

117|
    118|
  • Some hospitals provide medical interpretation as part of their international services
    • 119|
  • Third-party medical interpretation services exist in major cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou)
    • 120|
  • Interpretation quality varies widely — ask for credentials and experience
    • 121|
  • Remote (phone/video) interpretation is increasingly available
    • 122|
123| 124|
125|

💡 Key Distinction

126|

A hospital coordinator who speaks English is not a medical interpreter. For consultations, treatments, and informed consent processes, insist on qualified medical interpretation. This is a patient safety non-negotiable.

127|
128|
129| 130|
131|

3. What a Patient Coordinator Does

132|

A professional patient coordinator (sometimes called a medical concierge or patient advocate) handles the practical and communicative aspects of your visit that hospitals don't cover. Their value includes:

133|
    134|
  • Pre-trip: Confirming appointments, collecting records, explaining what to bring
    • 135|
  • At arrival: Meeting you at the airport, hospital orientation
    • 136|
  • During treatment: Attending consultations as your interpreter-adviser, helping you ask the right questions
    • 137|
  • Administrative: Managing billing, communicating with insurance if applicable
    • 138|
  • Post-treatment: Medication explanations, discharge process, follow-up scheduling
    • 139|
140|
141| 142|
143|

4. How to Arrange Coordination Services

144|

Most hospitals' international departments can recommend trusted coordination services. You can also arrange independent coordinators — look for services that:

145|
    146|
  • Have established relationships with the specific hospital you're visiting
    • 147|
  • Provide both interpretation and coordination (not just translation)
    • 148|
  • Can be contacted before, during, and after your trip
    • 149|
  • Have clear, written pricing — avoid verbal agreements
    • 150|
151|
152| 153|
154|

⚠️ Cost Note

155|

Medical interpretation and coordination services are not included in hospital fees. Budget for these as separate line items. Quality coordinators typically charge a flat coordination fee or daily rate. Get the fee structure in writing before committing.
